fact_text: Pakistan is described as the world's fourth-largest milk producer, at roughly 72 million metric tonnes a year, about 60% buffalo milk and 40% cow milk.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Around 92 to 94% of milk sold in Pakistan is loose (unpackaged), leaving packaged milk with only about 6 to 8% of the market.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because packaged milk holds such a small share, a standardised packaged-milk industry under a supportive policy environment has large room to grow.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Packaged-milk makers have traditionally bought from milkmen, so fresh, temperature-controlled milk from corporate farms can sell readily to them.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A mature-size heifer weighing about 600 to 700 kg eats roughly 3 to 4% of its body weight daily, about 25 kg of feed of which 10 to 12 kg is dry matter.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pregnant heifers need about four months of feeding before milking starts, so feed is a large cost during rearing before any milk is sold.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A herd of about 100 heifers needs roughly 8,000 sq ft of space before adding sheds, a milking parlour and other infrastructure.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: One acre of fertile land can grow enough fodder for about three to four cows, which is why dairy farms buy land to grow in-house feed as feed prices and quality become a problem.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A dairy cow's milking life is about five years, and corporate farms use artificial insemination to raise the share of female calves, which can replace herd animals or be sold for cash.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Milk yield per cow naturally declines after about the fourth year, so herd output depends on keeping animals healthy and productive across lactation cycles.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's rule of thumb is about 10,000 litres per heifer per lactation cycle, with actual output driven by genetics, feed quality and herd management.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Ghani Dairies runs a corporate dairy farm at Nurpur Thal near Khushab, and its main customers named in the video are Nestle, IRC (Interloop's dairy company) and Fauji Foods.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Ghani Dairies owns about 54 acres of land for growing its own fodder, which the analyst estimates can cover about 10 to 20% of its feed needs.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Management plans to raise milk output to about 37 million litres (around 38,000 tonnes) by 2028, though actual output depends on market and farm conditions.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Using the company's IPO documents, the analyst estimates Ghani Dairies' 2028 gross margin at around 16%, assuming modest milk-price inflation.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The same IPO-based estimate puts Ghani Dairies' 2028 net margin at around 12%, under the same milk-price inflation assumption.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In Ghani Dairies' FY25 income statement, revenue from contracts with customers is the milk actually sold to buyers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Gain on initial recognition of milk is added to revenue and then deducted in cost of sales, so its net effect is zero and it can be ignored.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The unrealised fair-value gain on growing non-milking animals reflects rising animal values rather than cash, so it is excluded from cash profit, and a quarter with a large gain is not normalised earnings for a P/E.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For a growing company the analyst applies a normal P/E only once growth has normalised, using normalised production or earnings for that stage rather than the current peak.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: An asset-based cross-check values a dairy farm at the market value of its animals plus infrastructure cost, as a secondary method to the earnings approach.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: As a minority shareholder on the PSX, the analyst prefers earnings-based valuation and P/E multiples over replacement-cost or asset-based values, citing PSX's history of pricing businesses below replacement cost.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Food companies have historically traded at high P/E multiples, and the analyst expects growth as Pakistan moves toward pasteurised milk to meet health standards.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Formal packaged-milk producers pay sales tax and income tax on profits, while most of the loose-milk trade is informal and pays neither, so the tax gap favours loose milk.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A rise in sales tax on packaged milk squeezes both volume and per-litre profit, because the wider gap with untaxed loose milk pushes buyers toward loose milk; a cut would help the industry.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Higher interest rates or a heavier effective tax burden gradually reduce businesses' cash flows, reinvestment capacity and valuations, and easing them builds a medium-to-long-term growth environment rather than a short-term trigger.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Why Corporate Dairy Farming Is Growing in Pakistan. Ghani Dairies Limited!' (YouTube transcript, undated)
